findings.description: Pickle.loads() used in test file for serialization testing
findings.reasoning: This is a test case in a test file (src/test_typing_extensions.py) that tests pickle serialization functionality. The pickle.loads() is called on data that was just created by pickle.dumps() in the same test, with controlled test objects (self.bottom_type). This is not a vulnerability because: 1. It's in test code, not production code; 2. The data comes from pickle.dumps() of known objects, not untrusted sources; 3. This is expected behavior for testing pickle serialization support in the typing_extensions library.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: No dataflow analysis needed - this is test code with controlled data flow from pickle.dumps() to pickle.loads()
evidence.notes: All 21 findings in this query appear to be similar test cases in src/test_typing_extensions.py testing pickle serialization of various typing constructs (NoReturn, NewType, TypedDict, ParamSpec, LiteralString, Self, etc.). These are legitimate test cases, not production vulnerabilities.

findings.description: Unsafe eval() in get_annotations function allows arbitrary code execution via malicious type annotations
findings.code_snippet: value if not isinstance(value, str) else eval(value, globals, locals)
findings.reasoning: The eval() call at line 4034 evaluates string values from type annotations. When get_annotations is called with eval_str=True, any string in the __annotations__ dict is passed directly to eval() with potentially attacker-controlled globals and locals. This allows arbitrary Python code execution if an attacker can inject malicious strings into type annotations. The function is used to evaluate type hints, but lacks validation of the input strings, making it vulnerable to code injection attacks.

evidence.code_context:
return_value = {key:
            value if not isinstance(value, str) else eval(value, globals, locals)
            for key, value in ann.items() }
        return return_value
evidence.dataflow_analysis: The eval() call processes string values from the annotations dictionary (ann.items()). The annotations come from obj.__annotations__ which could be controlled by an attacker if obj is user-controlled. The globals and locals parameters can also be controlled by the caller via the get_annotations function parameters.
evidence.notes: This is in the get_annotations function which is a backport of inspect.get_annotations. The eval is only executed when eval_str=True parameter is passed, making the vulnerability conditional.

findings.description: Unsafe eval() usage in typing_extensions forward reference evaluation
findings.reasoning: This eval() call in the _eval_with_owner function evaluates arbitrary code from forward_ref.__forward_code__ attribute. When get_annotations() is called with eval_str=True on objects containing user-controlled type annotations, an attacker can inject malicious Python code that will be executed. The code is evaluated with potentially attacker-influenced globals and locals dictionaries, allowing code execution in the context of the application.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: The eval() argument 'code' comes from forward_ref.__forward_code__, which can contain arbitrary Python code strings from type annotations. The globals and locals parameters are passed from user-controlled context in get_annotations() calls.
evidence.notes: This is part of the typing_extensions.get_annotations() backport implementation. When eval_str=True is passed to get_annotations(), user-controlled type annotation strings are evaluated as Python code.
